newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli PM must go if indicted or convicted - polls.
newsitem.headline: Israeli PM must go if indicted or convicted - polls.

text.p: A majority of Israelis believe Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu must resign if charged or convicted in a corruption scandal, newspaper opinion polls showed on Friday.

The 47-year-old leader, elected 11 months ago with a margin of less than one percentage point, on Thursday rejected calls he resign while prosecutors weighed police recommendations he be indicted in an influence-peddling scheme.

A Gallup poll of 487 Jews for the daily Maariv showed 52.6 percent believed he must quit and call elections if indicted. A Dahaf Institute poll of 503 adults in the daily Yedioth Ahronoth showed 52 percent wanted him to resign if convicted.

"This government is not going anywhere. We are not going anywhere. We are staying where the people and history have put us," Netanyahu told cheering supporters at his Likud party's headquarters in Tel Aviv on Thursday.
Police this week recommended Netanyahu and three associates be indicted for fraud and breach of trust in the short-lived appointment of an attorney general.

Prosecutors pored over the 995-page police report again on Friday, keeping Netanyahu's political life in limbo as they considered whether he would become the first Israeli prime minister to face criminal charges.

They said they hoped to have a decision by Sunday, ahead of the seven-day Passover festival. State Attorney Edna Arbel said Netanyahu would not have to be questioned again but legal experts said this would have no impact on the decision.
On Friday, Netanyahu and his wife Sara paid their respects at the state funeral of former president and U.N. ambassador Chaim Herzog, who died on Thursday after an illness at age 78.
Sara Netanyahu stood by her man, telling Maariv in an interview: "I know my husband was not involved in any deal."

The question mark over Netanyahu's future overshadowed a peace mission by U.S. presidential envoy Dennis Ross, who met in Gaza with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Thursday and was due to meet Netanyahu on Friday afternoon.

In Washington, the White House vowed to press ahead with efforts to revive peace negotiations stalemated over Israel's building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem which spurred weeks of Israeli-Palestinian clashes.

"The president (Arafat) reaffirmed that the peace process could not continue while the settlement process continues, particularly in Jerusalem," Arafat's spokesman Marwan Kanafani told Reuters after the late night meeting with Ross.
Netanyahu was also to meet Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Viktor Posuvalyuk on peace moves.

The Gallup poll, with a 4.3 percent margin of error, asked what Netanyahu should do if charged: 52.6 percent said he must quit and call elections and 39.3 percent that he must go about business as usual until judges decide the case.
The remaining 8.1 percent did not know or did not respond.

In the Dahaf poll, with a four percent margin of error, 52 percent believed Netanyahu should resign only if convicted, 25 percent said now, and 20 percent if and when an indictment is brought against him. Three percent had no response.
Prosecutors could still ignore the police recommendation Netanyahu be charged over the appointment of Likud activist Roni Bar-On as attorney general three months ago.

Israel's Channel One television spurred the police probe by alleging in a report in January that a Netanyahu ally on trial for corruption, politician Aryeh Deri, pushed Bar-On for the job in hopes of winning a plea bargain.
The television said Deri had promised that in return, his Shas party would support Netanyahu's deal with the Palestinians to redeploy Israeli troops in the West Bank town of Hebron.
Netanyahu, who has called the allegations "nonsense", is under no legal obligation to quit if indicted, although jurists expected he would step down to conform with what one called "public norms".
His resignation would force a new election for prime minister.
Netanyahu's ruling coalition of mainly right-wing and religious parties could in any event crumble.

"Even if no one is charged, should it become clear that very serious things were done from a public and democratic standpoint, we'll not be able to go on backing such a government and will want early elections," Yehuda Harel, of the four-member Third Way in Netanyahu's coalition, told army radio.
